title: Moats: Why durable differentiation, not just advantage, beats commoditization (AWS case)
summary: Industries commoditize toward zero profit unless a company builds moats: advantages competitors cannot easily copy. Using AWS as the example, the essay shows how to turn a generic moat from a taxonomy into an explicit multi-year strategy with named costs and accepted downsides.

principles.text: Industries commoditize: competitors copy features and costs, converge, and compete on price until profits hit zero.
principles.quote: Companies copy the best ideas from each other, whether in features to attract customers or cost-savings to build profits, so they converge to similar products with similar cost structures.

principles.text: A competitive advantage is not enough; it must be durable, meaning hard for rivals to copy.
principles.quote: It's not enough to have a "competitive advantage;" the advantage must also be *durable*.

principles.text: Prefer differentiation customers value (higher prices and share); cost-structure differentiation is second best.
principles.quote: Best is product differentiation that customers value, because that should lead not only to higher prices (because customers cannot get the same value elsewhere) but also greater market share.

principles.text: Even in a commoditizing market, stacking several moats (scale, ecosystem, learning curve, brand, switching costs) avoids commoditization.
principles.quote: AWS has largely avoided commoditization. The proof is in the market-share and in the profit.

principles.text: Moats take years of consistent investment, so they must be the core of strategy, not left to reactive agility.
principles.quote: Moats don't appear quickly or by accident; they require consistent investment and prioritization over a course of years.

principles.text: Naming a moat is not a strategy; specify how you'll build it and the second-order costs and failures you'll accept.
principles.quote: A strategy that states "We will create switching costs" is not a strategy; it is a statement of what you hope will become true, rather than an explanation of how you will cause that to become true.
